title: Net revenue retention (NRR)
reading_md:
**Setting.** The examples use Business Care, the monthly device-support subscription Voltmarkt sells to small offices. Each business pays a monthly fee, its MRR (monthly recurring revenue).

**What it answers.** Whether the customers you already had a year ago now pay you more or less in total, with upgrades, downgrades and cancellations all counted. Typical questions: "What's our NRR?" and "Do existing customers grow over a year?"

**Formula (cohort method, 12 months).**

NRR % = 100 x MRR of the starting cohort in the end month / MRR of the same cohort in the start month

- The cohort is every business with MRR above 0 in the start month.
- In the end month each of them counts at its current MRR: higher after an upgrade, lower after a downgrade, 0 if it cancelled.
- Businesses that subscribe during the 12 months, and businesses that had left before the start month and come back later, never enter the cohort.
- The same result in component form: 100 x (starting MRR - cancelled MRR - downgrades + upgrades) / starting MRR.

**Worked example.** On 1 September 2025, 400 businesses paid €20,000 of MRR in total. On 1 September 2026 those same businesses pay €21,600: some upgraded, some downgraded and 30 cancelled (counted at €0). Businesses that subscribed during the year add €5,000, which is left out. NRR = 100 x 21,600 / 20,000 = 108.0%.

Including the new businesses would give 100 x 26,600 / 20,000 = 133.0%, which mixes new sales into retention.

**Reading the number.** Above 100% means the cohort's upgrades outweighed its cancellations and downgrades, even if many businesses left. Gross revenue retention (GRR) is its partner: it caps each business at its starting MRR, so upgrades cannot offset losses and GRR can never exceed 100%. Report both.

**Common mistakes.**
- Dividing total MRR now by total MRR a year ago, which counts new customers.
- Putting reactivated customers into the cohort.
- Reading NRR above 100% as "no customers left".

**What it does not answer.** How many customers left (logo churn), how fast new business grows, or whether the revenue is profitable. A high NRR can hide heavy churn when a few accounts expand a lot.
